issues.legal_issue: A prior order directing verification of competing claims to the required level of support must be interpreted in the context of the dispute it was intended to resolve.
material_facts: The Court had directed an independent verification of the eligible residents’ present support after competing developers each claimed to have the required support.
An independent secret-ballot exercise found that neither developer had the support of 70% of the eligible residents.
The Court found that the direction had to be read in the context of the rival claims and the applicable support threshold, rather than as a search merely for which developer had more votes.
issues.conclusion: The prior order was binding and required verification of which developer had 70% support; since neither did, the report did not entitle either developer to the project and the appeal had to be decided on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: A judicial order must be read as a whole and in context, not by isolating a phrase; judicial propriety requires a coordinate bench to respect an earlier bench’s order. The Court treated the earlier direction as an exercise of its power under Article 142 of the Constitution to do complete justice. No earlier case was cited for this issue.

predicates.special_court_order_for_verification: The court directed an independent verification to resolve a factual dispute between competing developers.
predicates.competing_developers_claim_required_supp: Each competing developer claimed to have the required support of the eligible residents.
predicates.neither_developer_reaches_required_suppo: The verification found that neither developer obtained the required level of support.

issues.definition: When a court orders verification to resolve competing claims to a required level of support, neither developer qualifies through that verification if neither reaches that level.

issues.legal_issue: The rehabilitation authority may remove a developer for failure to develop within the required time, including where the landowning society has delegated development authority to that developer and the residents are also the society’s owners.
material_facts: The residents owned the land through their cooperative society and were also its occupants.
The society had given the developer authority to act on its behalf, and the developer’s roles as agent and developer were closely connected.
The authority had issued the developer a letter of intent, and the developer had failed to complete the rehabilitation work within the required time.
The authority cancelled the developer’s development appointment and letter of intent after finding unjustified delay.
issues.conclusion: In these particular circumstances, the authority had power under Section 13(2) of the Slum Act to remove the developer and cancel its development authority.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2) of the Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971 permits the authority to entrust development to another recognized agency where approved plans or conditions are contravened, or development is not completed within a specified time. The time condition may arise from the authority’s letter of intent, an agreement, regulations, or a condition under Section 12(10); delay need not concern only a condition imposed under Section 12(10). Although action under Section 13(2) normally lies against the owner, the owner society’s position as the residents’ society and its delegation of authority to the developer made the developer’s roles inseparable on these facts.

predicates.slum_rehabilitation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns implementation of a scheme to rehabilitate residents of a slum area.
predicates.developer_has_authority_from_owner_socie: The owner society authorized the developer to act for it in carrying out the development.
predicates.residents_are_society_owners_and_occupan: The residents are both occupants of the land and members of the society that owns it.
predicates.development_is_unreasonably_delayed: The developer failed to carry out the required development within the applicable time without adequate justification.

issues.definition: Where an owner society has authorized a developer to implement a slum rehabilitation project, residents own the society and occupy the land, and development is unreasonably delayed, the authority may remove the developer.

issues.legal_issue: The authority that issued a development permission may cancel it when necessary to implement the rehabilitation scheme, even if its specific power to remove the developer under the applicable removal provision is unavailable.
material_facts: The authority had issued the letter of intent required for the development.
The authority found that the developer had unjustifiably delayed a scheme whose residents had suffered for many years.
The scheme’s implementation required the authority to take steps to secure rehabilitation.
issues.conclusion: Even if Section 13(2) did not apply, the authority could cancel its letter of intent under its statutory functions and duties.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3A(3)(c) and 3A(3)(d) of the Slum Act empower and require the rehabilitation authority to get the scheme implemented and to take acts necessary to achieve the rehabilitation of slums. The Court also relied on the authority’s power to cancel the permission it had issued.

predicates.slum_rehabilitation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns implementation of a scheme to rehabilitate residents of a slum area.
predicates.authority_issued_development_permission: The authority granted the permission under which the developer was to carry out the scheme.
predicates.cancellation_is_necessary_to_implement_r: The authority considers cancellation necessary to secure implementation of the rehabilitation scheme.

issues.definition: If the authority issued development permission for a rehabilitation scheme and cancellation is necessary to secure rehabilitation, it may cancel that permission.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative decision to revoke development rights cannot be based on an allegation that was not clearly stated in the notice requiring the developer to show cause.
material_facts: The notices to the developer raised delay but did not specifically allege that its development rights should be revoked for lack of the required resident consent.
A general reference to regulatory requirements did not clearly identify the consent allegation.
The authority nevertheless relied on lack of consent as a ground for revoking the development appointment.
issues.conclusion: The part of the authority’s decision based on lack of the required consent went beyond the notice and could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: A show-cause notice must clearly and unambiguously identify the allegations the recipient must answer. The Court applied this procedural fairness principle in considering the notice under Section 13(2) of the Slum Act and the reference to Regulation 33(10) of the Development Control Regulations.

predicates.administrative_show_cause_proceeding: The authority gave a person an opportunity to show cause before taking adverse administrative action.
predicates.notice_does_not_specify_allegation: The notice did not clearly tell the recipient that the particular allegation might be used against them.
predicates.decision_relies_on_that_allegation: The authority based its adverse decision, in whole or in part, on that unstated allegation.

issues.definition: In an administrative show-cause proceeding, an authority cannot base its decision on an allegation that the notice did not clearly identify.

issues.legal_issue: The required level of resident agreement is mandatory for consideration of a slum rehabilitation scheme, with the form of agreement depending on the applicable scheme and on any migration conditions.
material_facts: Under the earlier regulations, the scheme could be considered where more than 70% of eligible occupants joined the society formed for redevelopment.

Under the amended regulations, at least 70% of eligible occupants had to agree to join the rehabilitation scheme, and the developer or owner had to produce individual agreements as required by the scheme’s conditions.
The project was migrated from the earlier scheme to the amended scheme, and the authority imposed conditions requiring agreements with eligible residents.
The developer submitted some individual agreements but did not establish that it had obtained the required support.
issues.conclusion: The 70% level was mandatory under the amended scheme. Migration did not require individual agreements before the scheme was submitted, but the authority could impose conditions requiring them thereafter; the developer’s failure to obtain them was relevant to its delay and entitlement to relief.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the 1991 and 1997 Development Control Regulations, including Regulation 33(10) and clauses 1.15 and 1.16 of Appendix IV to the amended regulations. Under the earlier scheme, the required threshold related to forming a society; under the amended scheme, the threshold applied to agreement to the rehabilitation scheme and individual agreements. The Court found no clear provision requiring individual agreements before submission on migration, but held that the authority could impose conditions during migration and implementation.

predicates.slum_rehabilitation_scheme: The proceeding concerns consideration or implementation of a scheme to rehabilitate slum residents.
predicates.amended_scheme_requires_resident_agreeme: The applicable scheme requires agreement from the specified proportion of eligible residents before it may be considered.
predicates.required_support_not_obtained: The developer did not obtain the required proportion of eligible residents’ agreement.

issues.definition: A rehabilitation scheme subject to a required resident-agreement threshold cannot be considered on that basis if the developer fails to obtain the threshold support.

issues.legal_issue: A finding that a rehabilitation developer caused prolonged delay may be upheld where the record supports the finding and the developer has not adequately explained its failure to progress the project.
material_facts: The developer agreed to complete the project within a specified period but made little progress for years and completed only two rehabilitation buildings.
The developer did not earnestly pursue approval of further plans and failed to produce the required resident agreements despite repeated opportunities and commitments.
Restrictions affected only part of the land, and other circumstances relied on by the developer did not explain its failure to develop the remaining area.
The authority and the High Court both found the developer responsible for the delay, and the Supreme Court reviewed the record and found that conclusion was not perverse.
issues.conclusion: The developer was responsible for the delay, and the authority and High Court were justified in so finding.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated responsibility for delay as a factual finding supported by the record and reviewed it for perversity. No earlier case was cited for this issue; the Court considered the development agreements, authority communications, planning history, and the limits of the asserted impediments.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_delay_finding and rehabilitation_developer_failed_to_progress_project and asserted_obstacles_do_not_explain_delay and record_supports_delay_finding

predicates.appeal_challenging_delay_finding: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a finding that a rehabilitation developer caused delay.
predicates.rehabilitation_developer_failed_to_progr: The developer failed to make substantial progress on the rehabilitation project over a prolonged period.
predicates.asserted_obstacles_do_not_explain_delay: The obstacles relied on by the developer do not adequately account for the failure to progress the project.
predicates.record_supports_delay_finding: The documentary and procedural record supports the finding that the developer caused the delay.

issues.definition: On appeal, a supported finding that a developer caused prolonged project delay is upheld where the developer’s asserted obstacles do not adequately explain the lack of progress.

issues.legal_issue: A developer responsible for prolonged and unjustified delay and unable to establish the required resident support is not entitled to continue a slum rehabilitation scheme or obtain discretionary relief.
material_facts: The developer was found responsible for prolonged and largely unexplained delay in implementing the scheme.
It failed to establish that it had agreements or support from 70% of the eligible residents.

The authority had not specifically notified the developer that lack of consent would be a ground for removal, but the consent failure remained relevant to the merits of the developer’s request for relief.
The residents had suffered for many years, and the Court found both law and equity against the developer.
issues.conclusion: The developer was not entitled to continue with the scheme or to relief from the Court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the applicable consent conditions, including those in the letter of intent and authority communications, together with the developer’s delay and the equitable nature of writ relief. It distinguished the unnotified consent ground as a basis for the authority’s removal decision from the consent failure’s relevance to whether the developer itself deserved relief.

predicates.developer_seeks_to_continue_rehabilitati: A developer asks to remain responsible for implementing a slum rehabilitation scheme.
predicates.developer_caused_prolonged_unjustified_d: The developer caused a prolonged failure to implement the scheme and did not adequately justify that delay.
predicates.developer_lacks_required_resident_suppor: The developer has not established the resident support required for the scheme.

issues.definition: A developer seeking to continue a rehabilitation scheme is not entitled to do so or receive relief if it caused prolonged unjustified delay and lacks the required resident support.

issues.legal_issue: A developer cannot rely on resident agreements obtained through a materially false promise, and such agreements do not entitle that developer to continue the rehabilitation scheme.
material_facts: The alternative developer promised residents larger flats than the authority had approved.
The authority had not approved the promised additional area, and the developer did not produce evidence that the authority had accepted its proposal to fund the extra area from its sale component.
Residents agreed to the alternative developer’s proposal in the context of that promise.
The alternative developer did not obtain the required level of resident support, and the society had terminated its agreement with it.
issues.conclusion: The alternative developer’s agreements, obtained by a false promise of larger flats, were legally unconscionable and unenforceable; it was not entitled to continue with the scheme or obtain relief.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that consent obtained by misrepresentation of facts is not consent and treated the agreements as legally unconscionable and unenforceable. It considered the approved rehabilitation area and the absence of approval for the promised additional area.

predicates.alternative_developer_seeks_to_continue_: A developer other than the original developer seeks authority to continue implementing the rehabilitation scheme.
predicates.resident_agreements_were_induced_by_unap: The residents entered agreements after the developer promised a benefit that had not been approved by the relevant authority.
predicates.required_support_is_absent: The developer has not obtained the required level of resident support.

issues.definition: An alternative developer cannot enforce resident agreements induced by an unapproved benefit promise or continue the scheme when it lacks the required support.

issues.legal_issue: Valid consent to a rehabilitation scheme should not be freely withdrawn, and competing developers should be considered sequentially rather than through competitive bidding among them.
material_facts: The Court considered the risk that residents might change their support repeatedly and leave a rehabilitation scheme in continual uncertainty.
It accepted the view that inter-developer voting or bidding could encourage developers to offer inducements to residents.
It stated that the first developer’s scheme should be placed before residents and considered if it obtains the required consent; a second developer may be considered if the first fails to obtain it.
The Court treated the special verification exercise in this dispute as a departure based on the case’s unusual facts, not as a general precedent.
issues.conclusion: Consent once validly given should not be permitted to be withdrawn, and developers should not compete by bidding against one another; consideration should proceed from the first-choice developer to another only if the required support is not obtained.
issues.legal_principle: The Court agreed with the consistent view of the Bombay High Court that allowing withdrawal of consent creates instability and inter-developer bidding risks improper inducements and undermines rehabilitation. It distinguished the exceptional verification in this case from the usual process. No specific earlier case was identified by name.

predicates.ordinary_slum_rehabilitation_selection: The proceeding concerns ordinary selection of a developer for a slum rehabilitation scheme, rather than an exceptional court-directed procedure.
predicates.residents_have_given_valid_consent: Eligible residents gave valid consent to a developer’s rehabilitation scheme.

issues.definition: In an ordinary rehabilitation selection, valid resident consent is not freely withdrawable and another developer is considered only after the first-choice scheme fails to obtain the required support.

issues.legal_issue: The Court may use its complete-justice jurisdiction to direct a supervised process for selecting a capable developer and protecting residents where prolonged litigation has left them without rehabilitation.
material_facts: Residents had remained in poor living conditions for decades while the project and related litigation stalled.
The Court found that neither competing developer was entitled to continue with the project or obtain relief.
The residents were also owners of the land through their society.

The Court directed the authority to invite qualified developers, assess their capability and financial viability and the terms offered to residents, supervise implementation, and ensure rehabilitation.
issues.conclusion: The Court issued directions under Article 142 for a supervised selection of a new capable developer, with protections for residents and implementation oversight.
issues.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Constitution empowers the Court to make orders necessary to do complete justice. The Court used that power to address the unusual facts and prolonged failure of rehabilitation; it did not treat the special procedure as a precedent for other cases.

predicates.slum_rehabilitation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns implementation of a scheme to rehabilitate slum residents.
predicates.residents_have_waited_for_prolonged_peri: Eligible residents have remained without the promised rehabilitation for a prolonged period.
predicates.no_existing_developer_is_entitled_to_con: The developers already claiming the project have been found not entitled to continue with it.

issues.definition: Where residents have waited a prolonged time without rehabilitation and no existing developer may continue, the court may order a supervised process to select a new developer.
